newsitem.title: UK: UK gas competition heats up on Monday.
newsitem.headline: UK gas competition heats up on Monday.

text.p: British Gas Plc, one-time U.K. natural gas monopoly, will see its market share shrink further on Monday when 1.5 million households join the 500,000 already allowed to pick their gas supplier.

Fifteen companies have been licensed to supply in the phase-two counties, and competition is intense. Although many consumers are expected to switch from British Gas, there probably won't be a frantic rush on the first day.

Residents in Dorset and the former county of Avon will join those in the phase-one areas of Devon, Somerset and Cornwall in being able to pick and choose as part of the break-up of the once state giant British Gas.

"Companies are moving to smooth the peak," said a spokesman for industry regulator Ofgas. "There won't be that many switching on the day. It's not in anybody's interest to try and push people through on the day. It will probably be different after two or three weeks."
The second phase will be carried out in stages. After Avon and Dorset switch over, Kent and East and West Sussex join the pilot area on March 7.
Eastern Natural Gas, part of Hanson Plc, says it has signed up 40,000 customers already.
"Of these, the lion's share will be in phase two," a spokesman said.
A spokeswoman for British Fuels Gas Ltd said that they had signed "many thousands" of customers in the new counties, although she would not be more specific.
"People are more responsive and more interested in switching" in the second pilot area than in the first, she added. "The market seems to be more active."
Sterling Gas, part of East Midlands Electricity, was not willing to comment at all, other than to say it will be supplying the market.
"In view of the intense competition in the market, we do not want to say anything at this stage," said a spokesman.

The run-up to deregulation in the second area has been far smoother than the first time, Ofgas said. A spokesman said he believed there had only been one or two complaints recently about hard-sell methods.
Complaints about selling tactics of some Eastern Natural Gas sales staff was tackled in December by the dismissal of several employees and the introduction of a new code of conduct.

In run up to the first phase of the deregulation last year, British Gas said it had 1,500 phone calls from customers, many of whom had signed contracts to change suppliers without apparently knowing they had done so.

Deregulation of the gas industry in Britain has been under way since 1986 when British Gas was privatised. From December that year, all users of more than 25,000 therms a year -- in effect a small number of large industrial users -- were allowed to buy from different suppliers.
From August 1992, consumers of over 2,500 therms a year, including many small businesses such as restaurants but not households, were free to choose suppliers.

The first 500,000 households were allowed to switch from British Gas in April 1996. Ofgas says about 91,000 consumers have already switched off British Gas but this figure does not include the households which have signed agreements with new suppliers but have not yet started taking gas from them.
Ofgas reckons that about 20 percent of the total 500,000 households will have ended their supply contracts with British gas when their current contracts expire.
By 1998, all British households will be able to pick their gas suppliers.

The 15 companies licensed to supply gas in the second pilot area are: Amerada Hess Gas (Domestic) Ltd ; Beacon Gas Ltd; British Fuels Gas Ltd; British Gas Trading Ltd; Eastern Natural Gas (Retail) Ltd; London Total Energy Co Ltd ; Midlands Gas Ltd; Northern Electric plc ; Norweb Gas Ltd; Scottish Power ; Southern Electric Gas Ltd ; Sterling Gas; SWEB Gas; SWALEC Gas Ltd; and Texaco and Calor Gas, trading as Calortex.
